newsitem.title: FRANCE: Semi-official French money market rate lowered.
newsitem.headline: Semi-official French money market rate lowered.

text.p: France's semi-official overnight lending rate was trimmed on Wednesday, offering financial markets hope of more official interest rate cuts to come.

The call money rate was lowered to 3-3/16 5/16 percent from 3-1/4 3/8 percent, leaving the rate about one tenth of a percent above the intervention rate, which sets the floor for French money markets.
The small adjustment was seen as a technical move to keep the call money rate close to the intervention rate, which was cut by a roughly equivalent amount on Tuesday.

"The central bank is keeping alive hopes of further rate cuts," Ciaran O'Hagan, bond analyst at JP Morgan, said. "Either the overnight rate or the intervention rate are likely to fall again in January."

On Tuesday, the Bank of France resumed its policy of slow but steady official interest rate cuts by shaving the intervention rate to 3.15 percent from 3.20 percent and cutting its five-to-10 day emergency lending rate to 4.60 percent from 4.75 percent.
Call money is closely steered by the Bank of France as a third, unofficial rate alongside its two official rates.

The official rate cuts on Tuesday came earlier than expected but most economists had predicted the Bank of France would get back to easing monetary policy after a pause due to recent market turbulence.

The lowering in call money was seen as part of a general easing in France's rate landscape this week after European Union nations agreed last Friday to a budget disciplinary pact to ensure members of a single currency do not run excessive deficits.

The so-called "stability pact", which imposes fines for countries which let their public finances get out of line, was the subject of disagreement between Germany and its EU partners ironed out at an EU summit in Dublin.
In addition to the official rate cuts on Tuesday and the call money move on Wednesday, French commercial banks on Monday lowered their base lending rates by a quarter of a percent.
The Banks explained the move as a reaction to dropping market rates. It was also seen by economists as a statement of confidence that French market rates would stay low.
Call money was last lowered on October 21, 1996.
